summary:
We developed River Lifeline, an open-source platform that monitors and helps predict whether the riverside communities around Tefé (Amazonas, Brazil) can still reach the town by water. During severe droughts, rivers drop and these communities can lose their only route to Tefé, where they get food, fuel, health care and schooling. 

With every pass of the NISAR L-band radar, which can detect water through clouds,  forest canopy and smoke, we map each community’s water route and cross-check the result with Sentinel-1. Each community is then given one of four statuses: Connected (a route at least 60 m wide), At risk (a route narrower than 60 m), Isolated or No data. These are shown on a public interactive map. 

To move from monitoring to early warning, we added a forecast. A “river twin” combines 37 years of Landsat surface-water occurrence with 40 years of daily readings from the Tefé gauge to estimate the river level at which every point of water dries out. Running our routing algorithm on this twin gives each community the river level below which its route becomes at risk or is cut off, and where the cut happens. In a hindcast of the 2026 dry season, scored against 16 real NISAR passes, it would have warned 11 of the 13 communities that were cut off, with a median of 35 days’ notice.

New study areas can be added through configuration alone, with no code changes. As climate change makes Amazon droughts more extreme, this kind of monitoring matters more every year.
details:
River Lifeline answers which riverside communities around Tefé, in the Brazilian Amazon, can still reach the town by water, and which are about to lose that route. For each NISAR pass, a Python worker maps surface water from the L-band signal, checks whether a continuous water route still links each community to Tefé and measures its narrowest point. Each community is marked connected (at least 60 m wide), at risk (narrower), isolated (no route) or no data. Every result is cross-checked against Sentinel-1, which also corrects NISAR where its L-band confuses wet mud with water. A web map shows each community’s status and its history.

The early-warning module matches each pixel’s long-term water occurrence with the distribution of the Tefé gauge record to find the level at which it dries out. It then sweeps river levels in 10 cm steps through the same routing to find each community’s cut-off level. The river level is forecast by persisting today’s departure from its seasonal norm, with 10–90% ranges taken from the forecast’s own errors over 40 years. These ranges become isolation probabilities at 7, 14 and 30 days. In the 2026 hindcast, each forecast used only data available on its issue date. On the days the radar passed, the twin’s statuses matched the radar’s in 80% of 2,066 community–pass pairs. Weeks of notice let responders plan water and food deliveries before a community is cut off, not after.

We used NISAR GCOV products from ASF and NASA Earthdata, Sentinel-1, JRC surface water, OpenStreetMap and gauge data from ANA, Brazil’s national water agency. Processing uses Python 3.12 with NumPy and SciPy. The backend uses Java 21, Spring Boot and MySQL 8 with a hexagonal architecture, and the frontend is JavaScript with Leaflet. Everything runs in Podman containers behind Caddy on a Raspberry Pi, published through Tailscale Funnel. GitHub Actions builds the images and stores them on GHCR.

Most drought tools measure water levels or extent. We measure connectivity, meaning whether a navigable path still exists for a specific community, and when it will be lost, because that is what matters to the people who live there. L-band radar sees water through clouds, smoke and canopy that block optical satellites, and a Raspberry Pi shows this can run at very low cost.

We cared about reliability. Results are checked against a second sensor, and the system says when it has no data instead of guessing. The forecast is labelled experimental, kept apart from what the radar observed, and its limits are documented, such as width not being depth. The output is simple enough for non-experts, built on free data and open-source code. A new region needs only a folder of coordinates and thresholds.
